analysis.one_liner: Lets borrowers wipe out private student loans in bankruptcy like other debts.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the House Judiciary Committee on the day it was introduced, never received a hearing or vote, and died there when the 118th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Under current law, student loans can be erased in bankruptcy only if the borrower proves the payments are an 'undue hardship' — a very high bar. This bill would change that for private (non-federal) student loans: lenders would no longer get special protection, and borrowers could discharge those loans the same way they discharge credit card or medical debt. It applies to bankruptcy cases filed after the bill became law.
analysis.who_benefits: People struggling under private student loan debt who file for bankruptcy. Today they must win an 'undue hardship' lawsuit against their lender — a costly, uncertain process most never attempt. This bill would let them treat private student loans like any other unsecured debt, giving borrowers real leverage and lenders a reason to negotiate affordable repayment.

how_it_helps.text: Allows private student loans to be discharged in bankruptcy without proving undue hardship, removing the special protection those loans currently enjoy [S2][S3].
The change covers loans and educational payments that are not government-funded; federal loans backed by a government program or nonprofit would keep the current hardship rule [S3].
The amendment applies only to bankruptcy cases filed on or after enactment, so it would not reopen closed cases [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Private student loan lenders, who would lose their guaranteed protection from bankruptcy discharge and, with it, some of their leverage to collect in full. If passed, lenders would likely price that risk into higher interest rates or tighter lending for future students — the cost of the change would be partly shifted onto new borrowers.

drawbacks.text: The bill would apply only to private loans; federal student loans — the far larger share of student debt — would keep the undue-hardship rule, so most borrowers with government-backed loans would see no change [S3].

An honest supporter would acknowledge the trade-off: if lenders can no longer rely on protection from bankruptcy, they may raise rates or reduce lending to higher-risk students, and some borrowers might be more inclined to file for bankruptcy than to repay. Restoring equal treatment in bankruptcy and keeping student credit affordable pull against each other.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core change is fair on its face: private lenders are businesses, not a government aid program, and there is no obvious reason their debts should be harder to escape than a credit card balance. The cost is that some of that added risk would be passed to future student borrowers through prices. The bill's main design weakness is its narrow scope — it leaves the hardship rule intact for federal loans — and it never advanced far enough for Congress to weigh those trade-offs publicly.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the House Judiciary Committee the same day, and the committee never took it up, so it expired when the Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Rep. Steve Cohen introduced the bill on January 9, 2023, with four Democratic cosponsors, and it was referred to the House Committee on the Judiciary [S1][S3][S5].
The bill's only action after referral was the referral itself; no hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor vote is recorded [S5].
The 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025, without the bill advancing, so it died in committee [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Private student loan lenders keep the special bankruptcy protection the bill would have removed, and borrowers struggling with private student debt remain in the same position. Because the bill drew only five cosponsors, its death may reflect limited support as much as any opposition.

for.name: Reps. Danny Davis, Eric Swalwell, Julia Brownley, and Ro Khanna

against.name: House Judiciary Committee
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing, markup, or vote on the bill, leaving it to die at the end of the Congress

against.name: Private student loan lenders
against.role: Industry that benefits from the current undue-hardship rule
against.what_they_did: Have consistently opposed proposals to make private student loans dischargeable in bankruptcy, since dischargeability weakens their ability to collect in full

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and all five cosponsors were House Democrats, and no Republican cosponsored; no roll-call vote was ever taken [S3][S4].

industries.note: The bill removes the special rule that makes their loans nearly impossible to discharge, so a borrower in bankruptcy could erase the debt and the lender could not collect. Their financial interest is keeping that protection, which comes at borrowers' expense.

industries.industry: Student loan collection and debt buyers
industries.note: Debts that can be discharged in bankruptcy are worth less and are harder to pursue aggressively, so firms that buy and collect private student debt would lose value on their holdings.
